intro: Five themes moving drug development this week — a target class coming apart in atopic dermatitis, the incretin fight heading to court, and regulators, capital and access models all quietly rewriting their own rules. Refreshed every Monday.

narratives.headline: The OX40 axis in atopic dermatitis breaks — two Phase 3 exits in five months, and now a shared safety question
narratives.detail: Amgen's rocatinlimab (depleting anti-OX40) went first in March on a Kaposi's sarcoma signal; Sanofi's amlitelimab (anti-OX40L) followed in July, framed as insufficient differentiation over Dupixent. Sanofi's fuller rationale — citing mixed Phase 3 results and reported Kaposi's sarcoma cases — now hints the KS signal may sit in amlitelimab's own trials rather than being read across, which would turn two unrelated failures into one convergent target-class safety flag. Inmagene's non-depleting IMG-007 is the last clinical-stage asset standing on the entire axis, and it still has to clear both bars that sank the leaders.

narratives.headline: The incretin marketing fight becomes a lawsuit — Novo moves to enjoin Lilly's comparison ads
narratives.detail: Novo Nordisk is asking a New Jersey federal court to enjoin Lilly's comparative-efficacy advertising pitting Zepbound and Mounjaro against Ozempic and Wegovy — the first time the GLP-1 rivalry has escalated from press releases and marketing complaints to actual litigation. With the clinical race largely settled on both sides, the competition is migrating to the courtroom and the ad copy. Worth watching whether an injunction reshapes how incretin efficacy gets marketed.

narratives.headline: Approval stops being a finish line — Tavneos's EU reversal puts its US nod on defense
narratives.detail: CHMP moved to revoke Tavneos (avacopan) in Europe in June, and Amgen is now proactively seeking an FDA advisory-committee hearing to defend the US approval before anyone asks. Read alongside CHMP's split rare-disease week — a positive opinion for Minoryx's ALD asset against a negative for Zevra's Meplyffa some two years after its US clearance — the pattern is hard to miss: a marketing authorization is increasingly a revisable state, on both sides of the Atlantic. Sponsors are starting to defend approvals they already hold.

narratives.headline: Biotech financing goes venue-shopping — Hong Kong listings and Korean megadeals fill the gap
narratives.detail: A US biotech is pursuing a Hong Kong-first IPO, a second alternative-venue data point after Scribe Therapeutics' upsized $128.7M Nasdaq debut, while Samsung Biologics pursues a roughly $1.8B acquisition billed as the largest-ever by a Korean biopharma. With fresh US import tariffs now landing on generics as well, the capital and supply-chain map is visibly tilting toward Asia. None of it is a single-asset thesis, but the direction of travel is clear.

narratives.headline: Access-before-approval hardens into a template — Merck licenses alimatravir for LMICs pre-filing
narratives.detail: Merck has issued voluntary licenses for its long-acting PrEP candidate alimatravir to low- and middle-income-country manufacturers ahead of any regulatory submission, following Gilead's lenacapavir playbook almost step for step. Two sponsors running the same sequence starts to look less like goodwill and more like an emerging standard for long-acting prevention. The open question is whether it spreads beyond HIV to other long-acting modalities.
